findings.statement: The institution is the deployer of the AI system and must ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy for the customer-service employees operating it; this Article 4 obligation applies to deployers of AI systems irrespective of the system's risk classification.

The described use — assisting customer-service employees — matches no use case listed in Annex III, so the system is not classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) on these facts and the AI Act's high-risk deployer regime does not attach as described.

The external technology company, as provider of a system that generates synthetic text, must ensure the outputs of the system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated under Article 50(2).

As the provider of a general-purpose AI model, the external technology company must keep technical documentation, make information available to downstream providers, operate a copyright policy and publish a training-content summary under Article 53(1) — the principal upstream-transparency lever available to the institution given its limited operational visibility.

The AI-assisted processing of customer conversations containing personal data and account information requires a lawful basis under Article 6(1) and must be limited to what is necessary under the data-minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c).

The AI provider and the cloud host process customer conversations on the institution's behalf as processor and sub-processor; the AI provider may engage the cloud host only with the institution's prior specific or general written authorisation under Article 28(2), and the same data-protection obligations must be imposed on the cloud host by contract under Article 28(4).

The institution may use the AI provider as processor only where it provides sufficient guarantees of implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 28(1), and must bind it by a written contract containing the Article 28(3) terms, including documented instructions, confidentiality and security requirements.

The institution must implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures for the conversation data — which may include account information — as processed through the externally operated, cloud-hosted service, under Article 32(1).

If the generative processing of customer conversations is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the institution must carry out a data protection impact assessment prior to the processing under Article 35(1).

Any transfer of customer conversations to a third country outside the EEA may take place only under the conditions of Chapter V of the GDPR; absent an adequacy decision, the institution must provide appropriate safeguards such as those under Article 46(2) before such a transfer.

As a financial entity within DORA's scope under Article 2(1), the institution must maintain a sound, comprehensive and documented ICT risk-management framework as part of its internal governance under Article 5(1).

The institution may use the AI provider and the cloud host only under contractual arrangements stipulating that they are not entitled to use the institution's data — including customer conversations — for their own purposes, such as model training by means of artificial intelligence, unless otherwise agreed, as required by Article 28(1)(b).

The contractual arrangements must stipulate all locations where the AI service is provided, including non-EU locations, the locations where conversation data is held, and information on the sub-contracting chain behind the hosted service, as required by Article 28(2)(a) and Article 28(2)(b).

The contractual arrangements must oblige the providers to allow the institution to inspect and audit their performance of the ICT services, including requesting information on sub-contracted ICT services — the contractual answer to the limited visibility described — under Article 28(2)(m).

The institution must report the Article 28(2) contract information for all its ICT third-party arrangements, including the AI service and its hosting chain, to its competent authorities in the register of information under Article 28(3).

Where the AI service supports a critical or important function of the institution, the arrangement must additionally include pre-contractual due diligence under Article 29(1) and contract provisions on concentration risk covering the provider's dependence on sub-contracted providers, termination rights and exit strategies under Article 30(1).

summaries.relevance: The one AI Act duty that reaches the institution unconditionally as deployer; it grounds the staff-side conclusion whatever the system's risk classification turns out to be.
With Annex III it fixes the route by which the high-risk regime could engage, and shows the described customer-service use does not trigger it — which determines which AI Act duties apply.
The closed list of high-risk use cases against which the deployment is measured; its silence on customer-service assistance keeps the system outside the high-risk regime on the stated facts.
Places the synthetic-output marking duty on the external provider, defining the transparency the institution can expect when AI-generated text reaches its customers.

Fixes the upstream obligations of the external technology company as general-purpose AI model provider, making upstream documentation and information a lever against the institution's limited visibility.
Bounds what the system may draw from conversations that may carry account details, complementing the lawfulness analysis of the processing question.
The threshold condition for all AI-assisted processing of customer conversations; no part of the GDPR analysis proceeds without it.
Conditions the institution's engagement of the AI provider as processor on sufficient guarantees, the entry point for controlling the processing chain.
Decisive for the two-tier setup in the scenario: the cloud host behind the AI service is a sub-processor that needs the institution's prior authorisation.
Defines the mandatory contract content through which the institution channels instructions and controls to the AI provider.
Carries the processor obligations down to the cloud host, closing the contractual chain the hosting arrangement creates.
Sets the security standard for conversation data that may include account information across a service the institution runs with limited visibility.
Adds the pre-processing impact-assessment step if the generative deployment over customer conversations reaches the high-risk threshold.
The gatekeeper for the transfer sub-question: conversation data may leave the EEA only under Chapter V conditions.
Provides the appropriate-safeguards route where no adequacy decision covers the destination — the practical compliance path for any transfer.
Fixes DORA's personal scope, on which everything DORA-side depends given the scenario's generic description of the institution.
Requires the governance framework into which the AI and cloud arrangements must be integrated, framing how the institution manages its reliance on external providers.

The most scenario-specific rule in play: it forces the contracts to exclude the providers' own use of the institution's data, including by means of artificial intelligence — directly aimed at the generative-AI setup.
Forces contractual disclosure of service locations, including non-EU locations, and of the sub-contracting chain, compensating for the institution's limited visibility.
Forces contractual disclosure of where data is held — the fact base for the EEA-transfer analysis.
Creates the audit and inspection rights that answer the scenario's limited-visibility problem contractually.
Brings the arrangements into the regulatory record via the register of information, securing supervisory oversight of the AI and cloud chain.
Adds pre-contractual due diligence where the service backs critical or important functions of the institution.
Adds concentration-risk, sub-contracting-dependency and exit-strategy terms for critical or important functions, matching the multi-provider chain in the scenario.

actions: Verify whether the institution is a financial entity within DORA Article 2(1), since the scenario describes it only as a European financial institution.

Confirm the system's actual functionality against Annex III — in particular whether anything resembling creditworthiness evaluation or scoring of customers occurs — since that would change the Article 6(2) classification and engage the high-risk deployer regime.

Settle the controller/processor allocation in the actual contracts, including whether the AI provider engages the cloud host as a sub-processor requiring prior written authorisation under GDPR Article 28(2) and Article 28(4).

Establish whether customer conversations are in fact stored, accessed or supported outside the EEA — the scenario leaves this open, and GDPR Chapter V (Article 44) turns on it; DORA Article 28(2)(a) and (b) require the contract to disclose the locations and sub-contracting chain.
Determine whether the AI service supports a critical or important function of the institution, which conditions the additional DORA duties under Article 29(1) and Article 30(1).
